samples.title: Synthetic: low back pain (Lisa) — onset not asked
samples.description: Hand-written synthetic consultation. Onset (when it started) is never discussed.
samples.transcript:
[Doctor]: Hello, Lisa. How are you feeling today? What seems to be the problem?
[Patient]: Hi, doctor. I've been having some back pain, especially in my lower back.
[Doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, or more like muscle stiffness?
[Patient]: It's mostly a dull pain, but sometimes I get a sharp feeling when I bend forward.
[Doctor]: Where exactly do you feel it? Is it in the middle of your lower back or more on one side?
[Patient]: Mostly in the middle, just above my hips.
[Doctor]: How severe is the pain on a scale from zero to ten?
[Patient]: Around a six, sometimes seven when it's really bad.
[Doctor]: Does the pain stay constant, or does it come and go?
[Patient]: It comes and goes throughout the day. Some days are better than others.
[Doctor]: Have you noticed anything that makes it worse or better?
[Patient]: Sitting for a long time makes it worse. Walking around and lying down usually help.
[Doctor]: Have you experienced any other symptoms, such as numbness, tingling, or weakness in your legs?
[Patient]: Sometimes I feel a little tingling in my right leg, but I don't have any weakness.
[Doctor]: Have you had any problems controlling your bladder or bowel movements?
[Patient]: No, nothing like that.
[Doctor]: Have you experienced fever, unexplained weight loss, or any recent injuries?
[Patient]: No, I haven't.
[Doctor]: Have you had similar back problems in the past?
[Patient]: Yes, occasionally, especially after lifting heavy things.
[Doctor]: Are you currently taking any medication?
[Patient]: I've been taking ibuprofen occasionally, and it helps a little.
[Doctor]: Do you have any medical conditions or medication allergies?
[Patient]: No, I'm generally healthy, and I don't have any known allergies.
[Doctor]: What do you do for work? Do you spend a lot of time sitting?
[Patient]: Yes, I'm an office administrator, so I sit at a desk for most of the day.
[Doctor]: I see. Let me examine your back and check your leg strength, sensation, and reflexes. Your examination shows some tenderness in the lower back muscles, but your leg strength and reflexes are normal. I don't find any major abnormalities.
[Patient]: So, what do you think is wrong?
[Doctor]: It may be mechanical lower back pain, possibly related to muscle strain and prolonged sitting. The tingling in your right leg means we should also monitor for possible nerve irritation.
[Patient]: Do I need an X-ray?
[Doctor]: Not necessarily at this stage. Imaging is usually not needed immediately unless there are concerning symptoms or the examination suggests a more serious problem.
[Patient]: What can I do to make it better?
[Doctor]: Try to stay active with gentle walking, avoid heavy lifting for now, and take regular breaks from sitting. We can also discuss suitable pain relief and physiotherapy if the symptoms continue.
[Patient]: Should I be worried about the tingling?
[Doctor]: If it becomes worse, or you develop increasing leg weakness, contact us promptly. If you experience difficulty controlling your bladder or bowel, numbness around the groin, or severe sudden weakness in your legs, seek emergency medical attention immediately.
[Patient]: Okay. When should I come back?
[Doctor]: Let's arrange a follow-up appointment in two weeks to see how you're progressing. If the pain gets worse before then, contact us earlier.
[Patient]: That sounds good. Thank you, doctor.
[Doctor]: You're welcome, Lisa. Take care, and I hope you feel better soon.
[Patient]: Goodbye.
[Doctor]: Goodbye.

samples.transcript:
[Doctor]: Hello, David. Nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
[Patient]: Hi, doctor. I've been having some pain in my right knee, especially when I walk or climb stairs.
[Doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, or more like pressure?
[Patient]: It's mostly a dull ache, but sometimes I get a sharp pain when I bend my knee.
[Doctor]: Where exactly is the pain located? Is it around the kneecap or more towards the back of your knee?
[Patient]: Mostly around the front of my knee, just below the kneecap.
[Doctor]: How would you rate the pain from zero to ten?
[Patient]: Around a six, especially when I'm using the stairs.
[Doctor]: Does the pain stay there all the time, or does it come and go?
[Patient]: It comes and goes. When I'm resting, it's usually much better.
[Doctor]: Have you noticed any swelling or redness around the knee?
[Patient]: Yes, it's slightly swollen, but I haven't noticed any redness.
[Doctor]: Have you experienced any stiffness, difficulty bending your knee, or a feeling that the knee might give way?
[Patient]: Yes, it's a little stiff in the morning, and sometimes it feels unstable when I walk downstairs.
[Doctor]: Does anything make the pain better or worse?
[Patient]: Walking for a long time and climbing stairs make it worse. Resting and putting an ice pack on it seem to help.
[Doctor]: Have you experienced any fever or felt generally unwell?
[Patient]: No, I feel fine otherwise.
[Doctor]: Have you had any recent injuries or accidents involving your knee?
[Patient]: No, I haven't had any accidents.
[Doctor]: Are you currently taking any medication?
[Patient]: I've taken ibuprofen a couple of times, and it helped with the pain.
[Doctor]: Do you have any medical conditions or known allergies?
[Patient]: No, I'm generally healthy, and I don't have any known allergies.
[Doctor]: Do you exercise regularly or participate in any sports?
[Patient]: I play football twice a week, and I also go running occasionally.
[Doctor]: Okay. Let me examine your knee. I can see some mild swelling around the joint, and there's tenderness around the kneecap. Your knee movement is slightly uncomfortable, but you can still bend and straighten it. There is no obvious redness or significant warmth.
[Patient]: Does that mean something is damaged?
[Doctor]: Not necessarily. Your symptoms could be related to irritation around the kneecap or an overuse injury. We should assess the knee further if the symptoms don't improve.
[Patient]: Do I need an X-ray?
[Doctor]: Based on today's examination, we don't necessarily need one immediately. We can start with conservative treatment and reconsider imaging if needed.
[Patient]: What should I do to help it recover?
[Doctor]: I recommend reducing activities that put extra pressure on your knee, especially running and football for now. You can use ice for short periods, avoid prolonged standing, and consider physiotherapy to strengthen the muscles around your knee.
[Patient]: Can I still go for walks?
[Doctor]: Gentle walking is fine as long as it doesn't significantly increase the pain. Try to avoid pushing yourself too hard.
[Patient]: How long will it take to get better?
[Doctor]: It depends on the cause, but you should hopefully notice some improvement over the next couple of weeks. If the swelling increases, the knee becomes red or hot, you develop a fever, or you cannot put weight on your leg, seek medical attention promptly.
[Patient]: Okay. Should I come back if it doesn't improve?
[Doctor]: Yes, let's arrange a follow-up appointment in two weeks. If the pain gets worse before then, contact us earlier.
[Patient]: That sounds good. Thank you for your help.
[Doctor]: You're welcome, David. Take care, and I hope your knee feels better soon.
[Patient]: Thank you, doctor. Goodbye.
[Doctor]: Goodbye.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Headache.

MEDICAL HISTORY

Patient reports history of diabetes mellitus type 2.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Patient reports she enjoys golfing.

MEDICATIONS

Patient reports taking metformin 500 mg twice a day.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Denies fever.
Eyes: Denies vision changes.
HENT: Reports ear flushing.
Neurological: Reports headaches and dizziness.

PHYSICAL EXAM

Eyes
- Examination: No papilledema.
- Extraocular Muscles: Grossly Intact without pain.

Neck
- General Examination: Mild posterior paraspinal muscular tenderness in the cervical spine and bilateral trapezius musculature as well tightness.

Cardiovascular
- Auscultation of Heart: Grade 3 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur that is unchanged from prior exam.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

1. Headache.
- Medical Reasoning: Patient presents with symptoms similar to a tension headache. On exam she has tension and tightness in her paraspinal muscles as well likely due to working at the computer. Additionally, I think her stress level is also a contributing factor.
- Patient Education and Counseling: I discussed the diagnosis with the patient today. I explained that her headaches may be caused by tension around the muscles around her neck and shoulders. I advised her that her symptoms do not appear related to signs of a stroke or brain bleeding. Questions were asked and answered today.
- Medical Treatment: She can continue to take Tylenol for the pain. Prescription for Flexeril 5 mg 3 times a day is provided as well.

2. Diabetes mellitus.
- Medical Reasoning: Due to her headaches, she has been inconsistent with her exercise and checking her blood sugar.
- Patient Education and Counseling: We discussed the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle. We also discussed the importance of keeping a watchful eye on her blood sugar levels.
- Medical Treatment: She will continue taking metformin 500 mg daily. Order for hemoglobin A1c, CBC, and CMP provided today. She will check her blood sugar daily and will bring that information in on her next visit.

Patient Agreements: The patient understands and agrees with the recommended medical treatment plan.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient will follow up in 1 month. She can follow up or call sooner if her headaches become more severe or suddenly worsen or she develops a fever.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Headaches.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Julie Jenkins is a pleasant 33-year-old female who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of headaches. The patient was referred from her primary care physician. The patient states that she was seen by Dr. White a few years ago and was going to obtain an MRI; however, Dr. White wanted her to see me first and urgently.

The onset of her headaches began when she was a teenager. Initially, her headaches appeared during menses, however she now experiences them more frequently and with more severity. Her pain is aggravated by physical activities. The patient states that she has been trying to exercise more in order to lose weight, however she is unable to exercise for prolonged periods of time secondary to the headaches. The patient locates her pain to the right side of her head and behind her eye. She describes her pain as a pulsing sensation. She also reports intermittent ringing in her ears for the last few months. Additionally, she reports intermittent blurred vision on the lateral aspect of her vision. She denies any numbness or tingling in her hands, feet, or face.

The patient enjoys running and wears either New Balance or Asics shoes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Neurological: Reports headaches. Denies numbness or tingling in her hands, feet, or face.

VITALS

Vitals are within normal limits.

PHYSICAL EXAM

CV: Normal head rhythm with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
NEURO: Cranial nerves I through XII are intact distally, including a normal cranial reflex.
MSK: Gait is normal.
Funduscopic exam: Positive for papilledema.

ASSESSMENT

Headaches, concern for idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

PLAN

After reviewing the patient's examination today, I have had a lengthy discussion with the patient in regard to her current symptoms. I have recommended that we obtain an urgent MRI of the brain to evaluate for any other condition that could be contributing to her symptoms. We will contact her to schedule this after approved by insurance. Once the MRI results are available for review and further discussion, I will also perform a spinal tap to evaluate the pressure in the brain. I have also advised her to be seen by a neuro ophthalmologist for a complete eye exam. Questions were invited and answered today. The patient agrees to the treatment plan.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient will follow up with me once the MRI results are available for review and further recommendations.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Low back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Bryan Brooks is a pleasant 39-year-old male who presents to the clinic today for the evaluation of low back pain. He is accompanied today by his partner.

Approximately 2 hours after he finished raking leaves yesterday, the patient began to feel a tightening sensation in his low back and tingling in his right foot. Prior to this, he recalls a similar episode approximately 3 years ago in which his symptoms resolved after 1 day. Ice and Advil provided no relief, but his pain is less severe when he is in a seated position and taking a hot shower helped alleviate his pain. The patient's partner reports that his pain seems to worsen when he stands up.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Musculoskeletal: Reports low back pain.

PHYSICAL EXAM

NEURO: Normal strength and sensation.
MSK: Examination of the lumbar spine: No pain on extension. Some pain with flexion. Pain with palpation around L5. Dorsiflexion is normal. Pulses are equal in all extremities.

RESULTS

X-rays obtained and reviewed in office today were normal.

ASSESSMENT

Low back sprain.

PLAN

The examination findings and x-ray results were discussed with the patient and his partner today. I recommend we treat this conservatively with rest, meloxicam, and formal physical therapy. If he fails to improve, we can consider obtaining an MRI for further evaluation.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient will follow up in 2 weeks.
